warmup.q: A hot loop in the report service calls block.millis() on every block of a document. For weeks only Paragraph and Heading blocks reach that call. Then Quote blocks start making up a third of all blocks. What does C2 most likely do with that call?
options: Nothing changes: the compiled code already handles any Block
It throws the compiled code away and recompiles the call as a plain virtual call, with nothing inlined
It inlines all three implementations, because they are small
It stops compiling the method and leaves it in the interpreter for good
warmup.why: C2 had copied both millis() methods into the loop behind type checks, and compiled "any other type" as an uncommon trap. The first quote trips the trap, the code is made not entrant, and the recompile sees three types with no 90% favourite. That makes the call site megamorphic: a plain virtual call each time, looked up at run time. It still works, just without inlining. The section on types shows this, and one twist about old tallies.

opening:
Back in the kitchen, the cook knows the favourites by heart now, thanks to two habits. When a recipe says "make the sauce on page 12", the cook copies the sauce into the main recipe, so the onions for both get chopped at once. And when nearly every customer wants fries, a basket of fries waits by the stove.

C2, the JVM's optimizing compiler, has both habits. It copies small methods into their callers, and it bets on the types that usually show up at a call. Then a customer asks for rice, the bet is lost, and the cook is back at the recipe card. Lesson 1 caught exactly that: readingMillis thrown away with made not entrant: uncommon trap when headings arrived.

None of this shows in your source, so it's easy to miss: a third kind of block, or a long error message, can change the speed of identical-looking code. In this lesson, we'll watch C2 copy one method and refuse another, count the types at a call, trip its bets on purpose, and meet the JDK methods it swaps for ready-made machine code. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a cook who copies short sub-recipes into the main one and keeps fries ready by the stove, until a customer asks for rice. C2 does the same: it inlines small methods within a bytecode budget, bets on the types it has counted, and falls back to the interpreter through an uncommon trap when the unusual order arrives.

Now look at a hot loop in your own code that calls through an interface. Count the classes that can reach that one call. Three or more, with no clear favourite, means a virtual call on every lap.

Next, we'll put all these timings on trial: why does a loop timed with System.nanoTime() report work that never ran?

sections.h: Inlining: copying a small method into its caller, within a budget
sections.html:
Start with something you can see. The report service checks every document it receives, and here's one check, written the way most of us would write it the first time:

Java
static long requireWordCountInline(long words) {
    if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) {
        throw new IllegalArgumentException(
                String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words));
    }
    return words;
}
Kotlin
fun requireWordCountInline(words: Long): Long {
    if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) {
        throw IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words))
    }
    return words
}

It looks tiny. C2 disagrees: it's 49 bytes of bytecode, the instructions javac writes into the class file, and that number decides whether C2 will copy it into its callers.

Inlining means C2 pastes the body of a called method into the caller and compiles the two as one piece. It's the cook copying the sauce recipe from page 12 into the main recipe. Skipping the call itself is the small win. The big win is that C2's other optimizations can now see both sides of the call. Escape analysis can prove that an object never leaves the method, so it needn't be put on the heap, the memory where objects live, at all. Constant folding can work out results from values known at compile time. Loop optimizations, such as unrolling (copying the loop body a few times so the loop makes fewer laps), can work on the whole loop. A method C2 doesn't inline is a wall it can't see through.

C2 decides at each call site, one call instruction in the bytecode, using the callee's bytecode size: the (N bytes) from lesson 1. The rule in HotSpot's bytecodeInfo.cpp is short. If the call runs on at least 25% of the caller's invocations (InlineFrequencyRatio), the site counts as hot, and C2 inlines methods of up to 325 bytes (FreqInlineSize). Otherwise the limit is 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). C2 also stops 15 levels deep (MaxInlineLevel), and it refuses a callee that is already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code (InlineSmallCode). These values are the same from JDK 21 to JDK 27.

The budget counts every byte, even code that almost never runs. Most of the check's 49 bytes build the error message: two boxing calls, which wrap each long in a Long object, an array for the arguments, and String.format. Move that cold path into its own method and the hot method shrinks to 21 bytes:

Java
static long requireWordCount(long words) {
    if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words);   // hot path: 21 bytes
    return words;
}

static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) {           // cold path, its own method
    return new IllegalArgumentException(
            String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words));
}
Kotlin
fun requireWordCount(words: Long): Long {
    if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words)    // hot path: 21 bytes
    return words
}

fun badWordCount(words: Long) =                                        // cold path, its own function
    IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words))

InliningDemo calls both versions from a method called summarize, each on 1 call in 8, so neither call site is hot. This is the real C2 output on JDK 25:

@ 15   ...InliningDemo::requireWordCountInline (49 bytes)   failed to inline: too big
@ 30   ...InliningDemo::requireWordCountSplit (21 bytes)   inline (hot)

JDK 21 prints the same decisions without the failed to inline: prefix. Don't read too much into inline (hot), by the way. It's simply what C2 prints when it inlines and has nothing more specific to say. The JDK's own code uses this split all the time: a small check, plus a separate method that builds the exception.

C2 counts the bytes of the error path too. Give the cold path its own method.

This check is a static method, so C2 always knows which code a call to it runs. Most calls in an object-oriented program aren't so simple.

try.title: See C2 refuse the big check
steps: Run InliningDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and keeps the lines about summarize and the two checks.
Find the decisions under the tier 3 compile (C1 says callee is too large) and under the tier 4 compile (C2 says too big).
Run the Kotlin twin. Compare the size of requireWordCountInline in both languages.

code.title: InliningDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Two versions of the same word-count check. One builds its error message inline, the other moves * the cold path into a helper. Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo * prints what C1 and C2 decided at the two call sites in summarize(). */ public class InliningDemo { static final long MAX_WORDS = 10_000_000L; // the error message is built right here, so its bytecode counts against the inlining budget static long requireWordCountInline(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } return words; } // same check, but the cold path lives in its own method static long requireWordCountSplit(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); return words; } static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) { return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } // a summary is about a tenth of the text; each check runs on 1 call in 8, so neither call site is hot for C2 static long summarize(long words, int i) { long r = words / 10; if ((i & 7) == 0) r += requireWordCountInline(words); if ((i & 7) == 1) r += requireWordCountSplit(words); return r; } static void work() { long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) s += summarize(1_000 + (i & 1023), i); System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), InliningDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { // keep the compile lines for summarize() and the decisions about the two checks out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("InliningDemo::summarize (") || l.contains("requireWordCount") || l.startsWith("checksum")) .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } }

alt.title: InliningDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of InliningDemo.java: the same two checks, compiled by kotlinc. // Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo prints the decisions in summarize(). const val MAX_WORDS = 10_000_000L // the error message is built right here, so its bytecode counts against the inlining budget fun requireWordCountInline(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) } return words } // same check, but the cold path lives in its own function fun requireWordCountSplit(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) return words } fun badWordCount(words: Long) = IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) // a summary is about a tenth of the text; each check runs on 1 call in 8, so neither call site is hot for C2 fun summarize(words: Long, i: Int): Long { var r = words / 10 if ((i and 7) == 0) r += requireWordCountInline(words) if ((i and 7) == 1) r += requireWordCountSplit(words) return r } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { var s = 0L for (i in 0 until 2_000_000) s += summarize(1_000L + (i and 1023), i) println("checksum $s") return } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.InliningDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "InliningDemoKt::summarize (" in it || "requireWordCount" in it || it.startsWith("checksum") } .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() }

try.expect: Both compilers refuse requireWordCountInline and inline requireWordCountSplit. In Java the sizes are 49 and 21 bytes. In Kotlin the version with the message inline is 66 bytes: "...".format(...) is an inline function, so kotlinc pastes its body (an Arrays.copyOf of the arguments and a null check) into the caller. The split version is 21 bytes in both. On JDK 25 each refusal starts with failed to inline:.

aside.title: Is Kotlin's inline the same thing?
aside.html: No, though the two are related. Kotlin's inline keyword makes kotlinc copy a function's body into each caller while it compiles your source, before the JVM ever sees it. C2's inlining happens later, at run time, and only for calls it judges small or hot enough. The two add up: bytecode that kotlinc pasted in counts against C2's budget for the method that received it. That's why the Kotlin check above is 66 bytes, because "...".format(...) is an inline function that brings an array copy and a null check with it. Use inline for small functions that take lambdas, where it saves an object per call, and keep big bodies out of hot methods in either language.

video.title: Inlining: C2 copies a small method into its caller, within a budget of 35 bytes, or 325 at a hot call

sections.h: C2 bets on the types it has seen at each call
sections.html:
Back to the documents. readingMillis from lesson 1 calls b.millis() on every block. That's a call through an interface, so it could go to Paragraph, Heading, Quote or a class nobody has written yet. C2 can only inline it if it knows which one.

The object a method is called on is the receiver. At tier 3, C1, the quick compiler from lesson 1, records the receiver types it sees at each call site, and C2 reads that type profile when it compiles. It's the cook's tally of side dishes, and C2 handles three cases:

  • One type seen: C2 inlines that type's method behind a cheap check, "is it a Paragraph?". The site is monomorphic, one shape. That's the basket of fries by the stove.
  • Two types: it inlines both, behind two checks (bimorphic). The profile keeps two types per site (TypeProfileWidth is 2).
  • Three or more: C2 inlines only a type that has at least 90% of the calls (TypeProfileMajorReceiverPercent). Otherwise the site is megamorphic, and C2 emits a plain virtual call, which looks the method up in the receiver's class at run time and jumps to it. Nothing gets inlined. The cook stops keeping sides ready and reads every order.

-XX:+PrintInlining shows the bet. This is the real decision for the millis() call in lesson 1's Hot, on JDK 21, while only paragraphs had arrived:

@ 27   workbench.performance.l01.Hot$Paragraph::millis (9 bytes)   inline (hot)
 \-> TypeProfile (1408440/1408440 counts) = workbench/performance/l01/Hot$Paragraph

Every one of 1,408,440 calls went to a Paragraph, so C2 copied Paragraph::millis into the loop.

What happened after the headings and quotes arrived surprised me. The recompiled readingMillis still inlined Paragraph, with TypeProfile (1463420/1572265 counts): 93% paragraphs. The profile is a running tally since the program started, and 20,000 trips through an article of paragraphs had piled up a lot of marks. On JDK 25, the run's last compile did switch to failed to inline: virtual call. The tally remembers the past, and what it says when C2 reads it decides the code.

To watch the number of types on its own, MegamorphicBench feeds one call site with 1, 2 or 3 kinds of block, in documents of 1,024 blocks. It's a JMH benchmark (lesson 3 explains JMH), and each case runs in a fresh JVM, so each starts with an empty tally. Two runs on the busy course machine, in nanoseconds per document:

types    run 1    run 2
1          950    1,170
2        2,093    1,547
3        7,913    5,122

The error bars on that machine were wider than the scores, so read only the shape: three types cost several times more than one or two. With the calls inlined, C2 can optimize the whole loop. With a virtual call per block, it can't.

Notice what didn't matter. A record is a final class, so Paragraph can't have subclasses, yet the log says C2 inlined it from the type profile, not from the modifier. Kotlin classes are final by default, and that changes nothing here either. What changes speed is how many types reach one call site.

So C2 compiles what its tally shows. What does it do about the orders it has never seen?

try.title: Count the types at a call site
steps: Predict the three numbers before you run: nanoseconds per document with 1, 2 and 3 kinds of block.

Run MegamorphicBench. Each case runs in a fresh JVM, so each starts with a clean profile. It takes about 10 seconds. On JDK 24 and later, JMH 1.37 makes the JVM print a few WARNING lines about sun.misc.Unsafe; they're harmless.
Run it with -Pargs='1 4'. Does a fourth type cost more than the third? The Kotlin twin runs 1, 3 and 4 types.

code.title: MegamorphicBench.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Benchmark; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.BenchmarkMode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Fork; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Measurement; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Mode; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.OutputTimeUnit; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Param; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Scope; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Setup; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.State; import org.openjdk.jmh.annotations.Warmup; import org.openjdk.jmh.results.RunResult; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder; import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; /** * One call site, fed 1, 2 or 3 receiver types (choose others with -Pargs='1 4'). JMH runs each case in a fresh JVM, * so every case starts with a clean type profile. Lesson 3 explains the annotations. */ @State(Scope.Thread) @BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime) @OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS) @Warmup(iterations = 2, time = 200, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Measurement(iterations = 3, time = 200, timeUnit = TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS) @Fork(1) public class MegamorphicBench { interface Block { long millis(); } // how long one block of a document takes to read record Paragraph(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 250; } } record Heading(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return 1_000 + words * 400; } } record Quote(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 300; } } record Caption(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return 500 + words * 200; } } @Param({"1", "2", "3"}) int types; Block[] blocks; // not final, and filled in @Setup: lesson 3 explains why @Setup public void setup() { Block[] kinds = {new Paragraph(42), new Heading(6), new Quote(30), new Caption(12)}; blocks = new Block[1024]; for (int i = 0; i < blocks.length; i++) blocks[i] = kinds[i % types]; } @Benchmark public long readingMillis() { long sum = 0; for (Block b : blocks) sum += b.millis(); // the call site under test return sum; // returned, so JMH consumes it } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { var builder = new OptionsBuilder() .include(MegamorphicBench.class.getName()) .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT); if (args.length > 0) builder.param("types", args); // for example -Pargs='1 3 4' var options = builder.build(); System.out.println("types at the call site -> ns per document of 1,024 blocks"); for (RunResult r : new Runner(options).run()) { var s = r.getPrimaryResult(); System.out.printf(" %s type(s): %8.1f ns (+/- %.1f)%n", r.getParams().getParam("types"), s.getScore(), s.getScoreError()); } } }

alt.title: MegamorphicBench.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // JMH benchmarks must be Java classes in this lab (the annotation processor runs on Java only). // This Kotlin twin runs the same Java benchmark through JMH's Runner API. import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.Runner import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.OptionsBuilder import org.openjdk.jmh.runner.options.VerboseMode fun main() { val options = OptionsBuilder() .include(MegamorphicBench::class.java.name) .param("types", "1", "3", "4") // one type, three types, four types .verbosity(VerboseMode.SILENT) .build() println("types at the call site -> ns per document of 1,024 blocks") for (r in Runner(options).run()) { val s = r.primaryResult println(" %s type(s): %8.1f ns (+/- %.1f)".format(r.params.getParam("types"), s.score, s.scoreError)) } }

try.expect: One and two types are close, and three types cost several times more: on the busy course machine, 1 to 2 µs per document for one type and 5 to 10 µs for three. Four types cost about the same as three (7.0 µs in one run): once the site is megamorphic, it's a virtual call either way. Expect wide error bars on any machine with other work running.

sections.h: When a bet loses: uncommon traps and deoptimization
sections.html:
C2 compiles what the profile showed and nothing else. A branch that was never taken, or a receiver type that never appeared, gets no compiled code. In its place C2 puts an uncommon trap, the stub from lesson 1. If the "impossible" case ever happens, the trap hands the running call back to the interpreter, the part of the JVM that runs bytecode one instruction at a time.

When a trap fires, the JVM deoptimizes: it rebuilds an interpreter frame from the compiled one and carries on in the interpreter. The compiled code is made not entrant, which means retired: no new call will enter it. The method goes back to tier 3 for more profiling, now with the new case in its tally, and is compiled again. In the kitchen, the customer who asks for rice sends the cook back to the recipe card, and soon rice is part of the routine. The figure shows the cycle.

DeoptDemo trips both common kinds of trap on purpose. It adds up the reading time of a document in three phases. First come paragraphs only. Then each document gets one folded block, such as a hidden spoiler, which costs the reader only a glance. Finally headings and quotes arrive. The loop body:

Java
long ms = blocks[i].millis();           // bytecode 16: which types has it seen?
if (folded[i]) total += GLANCE_MILLIS;  // bytecode 27: has this branch ever been taken?
else total += ms;
Kotlin
val ms = blocks[i].millis()             // which types has it seen?
if (folded[i]) total += GLANCE_MILLIS   // has this branch ever been taken?
else total += ms

The real log on JDK 25, trimmed to the important lines:

phase 2: one folded block per document
... DeoptDemo.readingMillis(...) trap_bci=27 unstable_if reinterpret
224   23       4       ...DeoptDemo::readingMillis (52 bytes)   made not entrant: uncommon trap
phase 3: headings and quotes arrive
... DeoptDemo.readingMillis(...) trap_bci=16 class_check maybe_recompile
255   26       4       ...DeoptDemo::readingMillis (52 bytes)   made not entrant: uncommon trap

unstable_if means a branch C2 had compiled as never taken: the folded block. class_check means a type check failed at a call C2 had inlined for paragraphs only. Each time, a new tier 4 compile followed within a few milliseconds, ids 26 and 37 in this run.

This is normal, and cheap when it happens a few times. HotSpot also caps how often one method can go around the cycle (PerMethodRecompilationCutoff is 400 recompiles). Expect a burst of deoptimizations just after a program starts, or when a new kind of input gets its first traffic. A steady stream of them in a service that has been up for hours is worth a look. JFR, the recorder built into the JDK, has a ready-made view for that, deoptimizations-by-reason, and lesson 5 uses it.

Here the picture breaks a little. A cook who gets burned by a shortcut might grow careful. C2 doesn't: it recompiles with the new facts and bets again, as boldly as before. That's usually right, because most programs settle into the same few cases.

C2 compiles only what it has seen. The first unusual input sends the call back to the interpreter.

Bets and traps are C2 learning about your code. For a few JDK methods, it doesn't need to learn anything.

try.title: Trip a branch trap and a type trap
steps: Predict: in which phase will the first made not entrant for tier 4 code appear, and with which reason in the deoptimization log?
Run DeoptDemo. It starts a second JVM with -XX:+PrintCompilation -Xlog:deoptimization=debug.
Match each trap_bci to a line of readingMillis (bytecode 16 is the millis() call, 27 is the if (folded[i]) test). Then run the Kotlin twin: its bytecode indexes differ, the story doesn't.

code.title: DeoptDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Adds up the reading time of a document in three phases: paragraphs only, then a folded block * appears, then headings and quotes appear. Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintCompilation * and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug, and the demo prints what happened to readingMillis(). */ public class DeoptDemo { interface Block { long millis(); } // how long one block of a document takes to read record Paragraph(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 250; } } record Heading(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return 1_000 + words * 400; } } record Quote(long words) implements Block { public long millis() { return words * 300; } } static final long GLANCE_MILLIS = 200; // a folded block, such as a hidden spoiler, costs only a glance static long readingMillis(Block[] blocks, boolean[] folded) { long total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < blocks.length; i++) { long ms = blocks[i].millis(); // call site: which types has it seen? if (folded[i]) total += GLANCE_MILLIS; // branch: has it ever been taken? else total += ms; } return total; } static void work() { int n = 1_000; Block[] blocks = new Block[n]; boolean[] folded = new boolean[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) blocks[i] = new Paragraph(20 + i % 80); long total = 0; System.out.println("phase 1: paragraphs only"); for (int r = 0; r < 3_000; r++) total += readingMillis(blocks, folded); System.out.println("phase 2: one folded block per document"); folded[500] = true; for (int r = 0; r < 3_000; r++) total += readingMillis(blocks, folded); System.out.println("phase 3: headings and quotes arrive"); for (int i = 0; i < n; i += 3) blocks[i] = new Heading(6); for (int i = 1; i < n; i += 3) blocks[i] = new Quote(40); for (int r = 0; r < 3_000; r++) total += readingMillis(blocks, folded); System.out.println("done, checksum " + total); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-Xlog:deoptimization=debug", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), DeoptDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("DeoptDemo::readingMillis") || l.contains("DeoptDemo.readingMillis") || l.startsWith("phase") || l.startsWith("done")) .map(l -> l.replaceAll(" pc=.*", "")) // drop machine addresses .forEach(System.out::println); } p.waitFor(); } }

alt.title: DeoptDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of DeoptDemo.java: paragraphs only, then a folded block appears, then headings and quotes. // Run it: a second JVM starts with -XX:+PrintCompilation and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug. interface KBlock { fun millis(): Long } // how long one block of a document takes to read class KParagraph(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = words * 250 } class KHeading(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = 1_000 + words * 400 } class KQuote(private val words: Long) : KBlock { override fun millis() = words * 300 } const val GLANCE_MILLIS = 200L // a folded block, such as a hidden spoiler, costs only a glance fun readingMillis(blocks: Array<KBlock>, folded: BooleanArray): Long { var total = 0L for (i in blocks.indices) { val ms = blocks[i].millis() // call site: which types has it seen? if (folded[i]) total += GLANCE_MILLIS // branch: has it ever been taken? else total += ms } return total } private fun work() { val n = 1_000 val blocks = Array<KBlock>(n) { KParagraph(20L + it % 80) } val folded = BooleanArray(n) var total = 0L println("phase 1: paragraphs only") repeat(3_000) { total += readingMillis(blocks, folded) } println("phase 2: one folded block per document") folded[500] = true repeat(3_000) { total += readingMillis(blocks, folded) } println("phase 3: headings and quotes arrive") for (i in 0 until n step 3) blocks[i] = KHeading(6) for (i in 1 until n step 3) blocks[i] = KQuote(40) repeat(3_000) { total += readingMillis(blocks, folded) } println("done, checksum $total") } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return work() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+PrintCompilation", "-Xlog:deoptimization=debug", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.DeoptDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "DeoptDemoKt::readingMillis" in it || "DeoptDemoKt.readingMillis" in it || it.startsWith("phase") || it.startsWith("done") } .map { it.replace(Regex(" pc=.*"), "") } // drop machine addresses .forEach(::println) } p.waitFor() }

try.expect: Phase 1 compiles readingMillis up to tier 4, including an OSR version. Phase 2 prints unstable_if at trap_bci=27, retires the tier 4 code and recompiles. Phase 3 prints class_check at trap_bci=16, retires it again and recompiles. On JDK 25 the PrintCompilation lines end in made not entrant: uncommon trap; on JDK 21 they just say made not entrant. In the Kotlin twin the method is 68 bytes instead of 52, and the traps sit at bytecodes 43 and 32.

sections.h: Intrinsics: JDK methods the JIT swaps for ready-made machine code
sections.html:
Some JDK methods never run as their Java code once they're hot. HotSpot carries hand-written machine code, or hand-written compiler instructions, for them. These are intrinsics, and they're the kitchen gadget that does one job perfectly. The recipe card may say "core the apple with a small knife", in twelve careful steps; a cook with an apple corer does it in one push.

In the JDK source, these methods carry @IntrinsicCandidate, whose Javadoc says the method "may be (but is not guaranteed to be) intrinsified". PrintInlining marks the ones that were:

java.lang.Long::bitCount (61 bytes)   (intrinsic)
java.lang.Math::addExact (32 bytes)   (intrinsic)
java.util.Arrays::equals (43 bytes)   (intrinsic)

Those are real lines from IntrinsicsDemo, the same on JDK 21 and JDK 25, and the report service has a use for each one. Long.bitCount counts the 1 bits in a long. The service keeps a document's text styles (bold, italic, underline and so on) as one bit each, so the count says how many are switched on. In Java it's 61 bytes of shifts and masks; on x86, C2 replaces it with a single POPCNT instruction. Math.addExact adds up the word counts of many documents and throws ArithmeticException if the total overflows, instead of quietly wrapping around to a negative number. Arrays.equals checks whether two uploaded texts have the same bytes, and ends up in code that compares many bytes per step.

The bytecode size doesn't matter for an intrinsic, because that Java code isn't what runs. Those 61 bytes are still there for a reason, though: they're the instructions for a kitchen without the gadget. The interpreter, or a processor without POPCNT, runs the Java version.

The practical rule follows. In hot code, call the JDK method instead of writing the loop yourself. A hand-written loop that compares two texts byte by byte gives up the many-bytes-at-a-time path that Arrays.equals gets for free, and it's more code to get wrong.

Kotlin gets the same intrinsics, because its standard library calls these JDK methods. ByteArray.contentEquals calls java.util.Arrays.equals, and Long.countOneBits() calls java.lang.Long.bitCount:

Java
long total = Math.addExact(totalWords, words);   // ArithmeticException on overflow
boolean same = Arrays.equals(textA, textB);
int styles = Long.bitCount(styleBits);
Kotlin
val total = Math.addExact(totalWords, words)     // ArithmeticException on overflow
val same = textA.contentEquals(textB)             // calls java.util.Arrays.equals
val styles = styleBits.countOneBits()             // calls java.lang.Long.bitCount

That finishes our tour of C2's notebook: it copies small methods, bets on types, loses bets and swaps in gadgets. We've judged every one of those choices with a timing. Which raises a question we've been dodging: how far can a timing taken by hand be trusted?

try.title: List the intrinsics in a hot loop
steps: Run IntrinsicsDemo. It prints the PrintInlining lines for the three JDK methods it calls.
Run the Kotlin twin, which uses contentEquals and countOneBits instead of calling Arrays and Long directly.
Optional: run the Java demo's second JVM yourself with -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and search for intrinsic to see how many others the JDK uses on its own.

code.title: IntrinsicsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l02; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.List; import java.util.TreeSet; /** * Calls three JDK methods that HotSpot replaces with hand-written machine code. Run it: a second * JVM starts with -XX:+PrintInlining and the demo lists the intrinsic decisions for them. */ public class IntrinsicsDemo { static long totalWords(long[] words) { long sum = 0; for (long w : words) sum = Math.addExact(sum, w); // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum; } static boolean sameText(byte[] a, byte[] b) { return Arrays.equals(a, b); // compares many bytes per step } static int stylesOn(long styleBits) { return Long.bitCount(styleBits); // one POPCNT instruction on x86 } static void work() { long[] words = new long[1_000]; // the word counts of 1,000 documents Arrays.fill(words, 1_999); byte[] t1 = new byte[64], t2 = new byte[64]; // two texts, as bytes long s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 200_000; i++) { s += totalWords(words); if (sameText(t1, t2)) s++; s += stylesOn(i); // bold, italic, ...: one bit per style } System.out.println("checksum " + s); } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { work(); return; } String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), IntrinsicsDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).redirectErrorStream(true).start(); TreeSet<String> seen = new TreeSet<>(); try (var out = p.inputReader()) { out.lines() .filter(l -> l.contains("intrinsic")) .filter(l -> l.contains("Math::addExact") || l.contains("Arrays::equals") || l.contains("Long::bitCount")) .map(l -> l.replaceFirst("^\\s*@ \\d+\\s+", "")) // drop the indent and the call-site index .forEach(seen::add); } p.waitFor(); seen.forEach(System.out::println); } }

alt.title: IntrinsicsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l02 // Kotlin twin of IntrinsicsDemo.java. The Kotlin standard library calls the same JDK methods, // so the same intrinsics apply: contentEquals calls Arrays.equals, countOneBits calls Long.bitCount. fun totalWordsKt(words: LongArray): Long { var sum = 0L for (w in words) sum = Math.addExact(sum, w) // throws on overflow instead of wrapping return sum } fun sameTextKt(a: ByteArray, b: ByteArray) = a.contentEquals(b) fun stylesOnKt(styleBits: Long) = styleBits.countOneBits() fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") { val words = LongArray(1_000) { 1_999 } // the word counts of 1,000 documents val t1 = ByteArray(64) // two texts, as bytes val t2 = ByteArray(64) var s = 0L for (i in 0 until 200_000) { s += totalWordsKt(words) if (sameTextKt(t1, t2)) s++ s += stylesOnKt(i.toLong()) // bold, italic, ...: one bit per style } println("checksum $s") return } val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") val p = ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions", "-XX:+PrintInlining", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l02.IntrinsicsDemoKt", "child") .redirectErrorStream(true).start() val seen = sortedSetOf<String>() p.inputReader().useLines { lines -> lines.filter { "intrinsic" in it } .filter { "Math::addExact" in it || "Arrays::equals" in it || "Long::bitCount" in it } .mapTo(seen) { it.replaceFirst(Regex("""^\s*@ \d+\s+"""), "") } // drop the indent and call-site index } p.waitFor() seen.forEach(::println) }

try.expect: Both programs print the same three lines, each ending in (intrinsic): Long::bitCount, Math::addExact and Arrays::equals. Kotlin's standard library functions disappear entirely: they are inline, so the call in the bytecode is already the JDK method.

compare.title: The same check, before and after the split

java.title: InliningDemo.java
java.html: // before: 49 bytes, "too big" at a call site that isn't hot static long requireWordCountInline(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); } return words; } // after: 21 bytes, inlined static long requireWordCount(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); // hot path: 21 bytes return words; } static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); }

kotlin.title: InliningDemo.kt
kotlin.html: // before: 66 bytes, "too big" at a call site that isn't hot fun requireWordCountInline(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) { throw IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words)) } return words } // after: 21 bytes, inlined fun requireWordCount(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) // hot path: 21 bytes return words } fun badWordCount(words: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words))

compare.note: After the split, both languages compile requireWordCount to the same 21 bytes, and C2 treats them the same. Before the split, the Kotlin version is 66 bytes against Java's 49, because kotlinc pastes the body of the inline format extension into the caller: an Arrays.copyOf of the arguments and a null check on the result. So the same fix matters a little more in Kotlin. In both languages the cold method still builds exactly the same message, so nobody searching the logs for it will notice the change.

worked.title: Find out why a hot method isn't inlined, and fix it

steps.say: The report handler is slower than expected in a profile. Start the service with the diagnostic flags and look for the check in the inlining log.
steps.code: java -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining -cp report.jar example.report.Main | grep requireWordCount

steps.say: C2's line names the method, its bytecode size and the reason. too big means the call site isn't hot and the callee is over 35 bytes. hot method too big would mean a hot site and a callee over 325 bytes.
steps.code: @ 15   example.report.Guards::requireWordCount (49 bytes)   failed to inline: too big

steps.say: Look at what the 49 bytes are. javap -c -p shows the boxing calls, the argument array and the String.format that build the message. All of that is the cold path.
steps.code: javap -c -p -cp report.jar example.report.Guards | grep -A 30 'long requireWordCount'

steps.say: Move the cold path into its own method and return the exception from it, so the hot method still ends in throw. Self-check before reading on: why return the exception instead of throwing it inside the helper? (Answer: with throw badWordCount(words), javac and the next reader can both see that the method ends there. A helper that throws by itself looks like an ordinary call that returns.)
steps.code: static long requireWordCount(long words) { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words); // hot path: 21 bytes return words; } static IllegalArgumentException badWordCount(long words) { // cold path, its own method return new IllegalArgumentException( String.format("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d", MAX_WORDS, words)); }

alt.html: fun requireWordCount(words: Long): Long { if (words <= 0 || words > MAX_WORDS) throw badWordCount(words) // hot path: 21 bytes return words } fun badWordCount(words: Long) = // cold path, its own function IllegalArgumentException("word count must be between 1 and %d, got %d".format(MAX_WORDS, words))

steps.say: Run the same command again. The hot method is 21 bytes and C2 inlines it. Keep the message text identical, because someone's alert or log search may match on it.

lab.title: Fit two hot checks into the inlining budget
steps: Open DocumentGuards, the two checks the report service runs on every document it receives: one for the word count and one for the title. Run the tests. Two pass (the checks behave correctly) and two fail: requireWordCount is 49 bytes of bytecode and requireTitle is 68. The limit in the test is 35, C2's MaxInlineSize.
Check the sizes yourself: after a build, run javap -c -p -cp performance/build/classes/java/main workbench.performance.l02.DocumentGuards. The offset of the last instruction plus one is the size.
Move the message building out of requireWordCount into a private static method that returns the exception. Keep the exact message.
Do the same for requireTitle. The null case must still say got null.
Run the tests until all four pass. The test reads the compiled class file, so BytecodeSize.java in the test folder shows exactly what it measures.
hints: The shape that fits: if (bad) throw badWordCount(words); return words;. Everything about the message goes in badWordCount.
String.format with two arguments costs a lot of bytecode: an array, two boxing calls and the call itself. In the cold method that doesn't matter.
In requireTitle, the title == null ? "null" : ... choice belongs in the cold method too. Pass the title itself to the helper.
Both fixed methods come out at 21 and 27 bytes in the reference solution.

drill.title: Split a check from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a check requireLanguage(String code) that returns code when it is exactly 2 characters long, such as "en", and otherwise throws IllegalArgumentException("language must be 2 letters, got '" + code + "'"). Shape it so the hot method stays small. Then write down the two C2 size limits and when each applies.

answer.html: static String requireLanguage(String code) { if (code == null || code.length() != 2) throw badLanguage(code); // hot: a check and a call return code; } private static IllegalArgumentException badLanguage(String code) { // cold: everything else return new IllegalArgumentException("language must be 2 letters, got '" + code + "'"); } // C2 inlines up to 35 bytes of bytecode at a call site that runs on fewer than 25% of the // caller's invocations (MaxInlineSize), and up to 325 bytes at a hot one (FreqInlineSize).

alt.html: fun requireLanguage(code: String?): String { if (code == null || code.length != 2) throw badLanguage(code) // hot: a check and a call return code } private fun badLanguage(code: String?) = // cold: everything else IllegalArgumentException("language must be 2 letters, got '$code'") // C2 inlines up to 35 bytes of bytecode at a call site that runs on fewer than 25% of the // caller's invocations (MaxInlineSize), and up to 325 bytes at a hot one (FreqInlineSize).

recap: C2 inlines a callee only within a bytecode budget: 35 bytes at call sites that aren't hot, 325 bytes at hot ones (25% of the caller's calls). Error paths count too, so give them their own method.

At each interface or virtual call, C2 uses the receiver types tier 3 recorded. One or two types get inlined behind type checks. Three or more without a 90% favourite become a plain virtual call. The tally counts everything since the program started.
Whatever the profile never saw becomes an uncommon trap. When one fires, the call goes back to the interpreter, the code is made not entrant, and the method is compiled again with the new case.
-XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:+PrintInlining and -Xlog:deoptimization=debug show these decisions. inline (hot) is just C2's success message.
Intrinsics (@IntrinsicCandidate) swap JDK methods such as Math.addExact, Arrays.equals and Long.bitCount for ready-made machine code. Kotlin's standard library reaches the same ones.

The limit: these logs explain one method at a time. They can't tell you which of thousands of methods is worth your attention; that takes careful measurement (lesson 3) and a profiler (lessons 5 and 6).

explain.prompt: A colleague asks: "Why did our report loop get slower when we added a third kind of block, even though the new class is tiny?" Explain it in your own words.
explain.answer: The loop calls millis() through the Block interface. While only paragraphs and headings reached that call, C2 inlined both implementations behind type checks, and could then optimize the loop body as a whole. It compiled any other type as an uncommon trap. When the first quote arrived, the trap fired, the compiled code was thrown away and the method was compiled again. With three types and none above 90%, the call site is megamorphic, so C2 now emits a virtual call for every block and inlines nothing. The size of the new class doesn't matter. What changed is the number of types reaching that one call. One twist: the profile counts everything since start-up, so if paragraphs had piled up 90% of the old counts, C2 might keep inlining them for a while.

deeper.html:
Inlining is what makes escape analysis work. C2 can only prove that an object never leaves a method if it can see every method the object is passed to. A small result object created in a hot method and passed to a callee that isn't inlined has escaped, so it gets put on the heap. The memory track looks at escape analysis from the allocation side.

For experiments, -XX:CompileCommand=dontinline,example.report.Guards::requireWordCount and -XX:CompileCommand=inline,... force a decision for one method, and the inlining log then says it was forced by CompileCommand. Use them to test a theory, not as a production fix.

Not every call through an interface is megamorphic just because many classes pass through it. Take a shared helper such as static long timed(LongSupplier work) that three callers use with three different lambdas. Once C2 has inlined timed into each caller, it can see the exact lambda class at each spot and doesn't need the shared profile. Megamorphic sites come from types C2 can't see at compile time, such as objects read from an array, a field or a collection.

Other messages you'll meet in the log: inlining too deep (more than 15 levels, MaxInlineLevel), already compiled into a big method (a callee already compiled into more than 2,500 bytes of machine code), hot method too big (a hot site, over 325 bytes) and no static binding (C1 can't inline a virtual call). JITWatch shows the same information per method if the raw log gets too long.
